The Envelope
Ramesh-ji steps out from behind the bikes, smiling with every gold tooth.
Ah! The cricketer! Your Papa owes me thirty thousand. The interest is... growing. Like you.
Step between them.
Brave. Risky.
Call Pandey-ji.
He knows everyone in this town.
"Papa, let me handle this."
Take charge.
Handle? You? Go inside, beta.
You stand between Papa and the goon. You are shaking. You do not move.
Brave boy. Brave boys break easily.
Pandey-ji arrives on his ancient scooter eight minutes later. In his slippers.
Ramesh. Class 6, Government Inter College. You copied my maths answers for two years.
...Pandey-ji. Namaste.
Two months. No interest. Or I tell your wife about the second phone.
Ramesh-ji's smile flickers. He nods.
But listen. I'm a businessman. Chauhan sahab tells me you need ₹25,000 for trials.
I lend ₹55,000. Papa's debt and your trial slot. Twenty percent a month. Everybody wins.
"Fine. Lend it."
Buy the slot. Bury the family in debt.
"No. I'll get picked on runs."
Clean. Harder.
"I have Chauhan's man on tape."
Use the recording.
Runs! Hahaha. Okay, hero. Runs.
Smart boy. Cash tomorrow. Interest from today.
Papa doesn't say a single word to you that night.
You hold up your phone. Press play. "...twenty-five thousand, cash, to Chauhan sahab's office..."
Delete that, beta. You don't know what kind of people you are playing with.
No. But now they know who they're playing with.
Saturday. Rajgarh Gymkhana vs Meerut Lions XI. Two hundred people. One borrowed scoreboard.
You're carrying the drinks. Over 17, the opener pulls his hamstring. Pandey-ji looks at the bench. At you.
Drinks down. Pads on. Now.
Last over. Rajgarh need 11 to win. Bunty Tyagi has the ball. You have the strike.
Eleven off six. I've already written the headline. Don't make me rewrite it.
11 off 6
Bunty Tyagi, Meerut's fastest. The whole maidan on its feet. Win it.
They carry you off the field on their shoulders. Somebody's uncle is crying. Somebody is still selling samosas.
I closed the stall. First time in eleven years. I wanted to see.
Lost. The Meerut boys celebrate on your pitch. The walk back to the pavilion is the longest of your life.
Every great one has a day like this. Most of them quit after it. Will you?
Monday morning. The district trials list goes up on the clubhouse wall.
Thirty-two boys crowd around it. You read from the top. Your hands are shaking.
Number one: Vikrant Chauhan. Of course.
Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen. Sixteen.
Your name is there.
But someone has drawn a line straight through it.
In red pen.
Who crossed out your name? And why does Neha always carry a red pen?
